title: What is the difference between `git reset` and `git revert` for undoing changes (`reset` moves the branch pointer and rewrites history — safe only on unshared/local commits; `revert` adds a new commit that undoes a previous one — safe for shared/pushed history), and what is `git reflog` (a local log of everywhere `HEAD` has pointed, used to recover "lost" commits after a bad reset/rebase)?
shortTitle: `git reset` vs `git revert`, and what `git reflog` is

s1_definition.profdef: `git reset` undoes changes by moving the current branch pointer to an earlier commit, effectively rewriting history, so the undone commits drop out of the branch; its three modes — soft, mixed, hard — control whether your staged and working changes are kept or discarded. Because it rewrites history it is safe only on local, unshared commits. `git revert` undoes a commit by creating a brand-new commit that applies the inverse of the target commit, leaving all history intact, which makes it safe for shared, already-pushed commits. `git reflog` is a local log recording every position HEAD has pointed to, letting you recover commits that seem lost after a bad reset or rebase.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine correcting a mistaken entry in National Bank of India's ledger. git reset is like tearing the last page out of the ledger as if it was never written — fine if only you have seen that page, but disastrous if other branches already copied it, because now the books disagree. git revert is the proper banking way to fix a posted transaction: you do not erase it; you write a new, opposite correcting entry that cancels it out, so the full audit trail stays intact. git reflog is the bank's internal CCTV log that records every move you made, so even if you tore out a page by mistake, you can look back at the footage and find exactly where that page was and restore it.
s1_definition.oneliner: reset rewrites history by moving the branch pointer (local only), revert safely cancels a commit with a new inverse commit (shared-safe), and reflog is your safety net to recover lost commits.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `git reset` undoes changes by moving the current branch pointer to an earlier commit, effectively rewriting history, so the undone commits drop out of the branch; its three modes — soft, mixed, hard — control whether your staged and working changes are kept or discarded. Because it rewrites history it is safe only on local, unshared commits. `git revert` undoes a commit by creating a brand-new commit that applies the inverse of the target commit, leaving all history intact, which makes it safe for shared, already-pushed commits. `git reflog` is a local log recording every position HEAD has pointed to, letting you recover commits that seem lost after a bad reset or rebase.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine correcting a mistaken entry in National Bank of India's ledger. git reset is like tearing the last page out of the ledger as if it was never written — fine if only you have seen that page, but disastrous if other branches already copied it, because now the books disagree. git revert is the proper banking way to fix a posted transaction: you do not erase it; you write a new, opposite correcting entry that cancels it out, so the full audit trail stays intact. git reflog is the bank's internal CCTV log that records every move you made, so even if you tore out a page by mistake, you can look back at the footage and find exactly where that page was and restore it.

**One line to remember:** reset rewrites history by moving the branch pointer (local only), revert safely cancels a commit with a new inverse commit (shared-safe), and reflog is your safety net to recover lost commits.

sections.s2_technical:
git reset moves the tip of your current branch to point at a different, usually earlier, commit. Because the branch pointer moves backward, the commits after the new position are no longer part of the branch history — this is a history rewrite. Reset has three modes that differ in what happens to your staging area and working directory. Soft reset moves the pointer but leaves both the staging area and working directory untouched, so the changes from the undone commits remain staged, ready to recommit — perfect for squashing or redoing the last commit's message. Mixed reset, the default, moves the pointer and unstages the changes but keeps them in the working directory, so you can re-stage selectively. Hard reset moves the pointer and discards both staging and working-directory changes entirely, matching the working tree to the target commit — this is the dangerous one because uncommitted work is truly lost.

The key safety fact about reset is that it rewrites history. If the commits you reset away were only ever on your machine, no harm done. But if you already pushed them and teammates pulled them, resetting locally and force-pushing removes commits others still have, causing divergence and potential lost work. So reset is safe only on unshared, local commits.

git revert takes a different, non-destructive approach. Instead of removing a commit, it computes the inverse of that commit's changes and records them as a brand-new commit on top of the current history. If a commit added a line, the revert commit removes it; if it deleted a line, the revert restores it. The original commit stays in history, and a new commit cancels its effect. Because nothing is rewritten and no existing commit changes its hash, revert is completely safe on shared, already-pushed branches — everyone just pulls one additional commit. This is the correct way to undo something that is already public, and for a bank it has the bonus of preserving the full audit trail: you can see both the mistake and its correction.

So the decision rule is simple. If the commit is still local and unshared, reset is fine and often cleaner. If the commit is already pushed and others may have it, use revert so you never rewrite shared history. For a mistaken merge that is already public, revert is the safe tool, though reverting a merge commit requires specifying which parent to keep.

git reflog is the safety net that makes Git forgiving. Every time HEAD moves — a commit, a checkout, a reset, a rebase, a merge — Git records the previous position in the reflog, a local log private to your repository. So even after a hard reset that seems to have destroyed commits, those commits are not immediately deleted; they are just unreferenced, and the reflog still remembers their hashes. You run git reflog, find the entry just before the bad operation, and recover by resetting back to it or creating a branch at that hash. A senior-level nuance: reflog is local and has an expiry — unreferenced commits are eventually garbage-collected after a default period — so reflog recovers recent mistakes, not ancient ones, and it does not exist on the remote. The practical wisdom I always share is that because of reflog, almost nothing you do locally in Git is truly irreversible in the short term, which should make you confident rather than reckless, but it is still no excuse for hard-resetting or force-pushing shared branches.
sections.s3_banking:
A National Bank of India engineer must undo mistakes in different situations and recover from a bad reset.

Problem 1 — the engineer made a bad commit that is still only local. This is exactly where git reset fits — move the branch pointer back to drop the commit cleanly before anyone sees it.

Problem 2 — a buggy commit was already pushed to main and teammates have pulled it. Rewriting history now would break their repositories. This is exactly where git revert fits — add a new commit that cancels the bug while preserving the audit trail.

Problem 3 — the engineer ran a hard reset and panicked, thinking a good commit was lost forever. This is exactly where git reflog fits — find the pre-reset position and restore the commit.

The mini-project is a git walkthrough: a soft/mixed/hard reset on a local commit, a revert of an already-pushed buggy commit, and a reflog recovery after a bad hard reset. An InterestPostingService Java class provides the real code being changed.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Inspect history and reflog at any point.
git log --oneline -5
git reflog -5

# After a revert, confirm BOTH the original and the revert commit exist.
git log --oneline | grep -i revert

# Run tests to confirm the undo produced correct behavior.
mvn test
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a local bad commit to undo, an already-pushed buggy commit to undo, and a good commit accidentally hard-reset away.

Step 1: The engineer has a local-only commit with a wrong 9% rate. Running git reset soft moves the branch pointer back one commit but keeps the changes staged, so the engineer can fix the rate and recommit cleanly. Because this commit was never pushed, rewriting history here harms no one.

Step 2: To see the modes, the engineer notes that mixed reset would instead leave the changes unstaged in the working directory, and hard reset would discard them entirely. Hard reset is only safe because the commit is unshared.

Step 3: Separately, a buggy commit that posted interest twice was already pushed to main and pulled by teammates. The engineer must not rewrite that shared history, so instead of reset, they run git revert on the buggy commit.

Step 4: git revert computes the inverse of the buggy commit and records it as a new commit on top of main. The original buggy commit remains in history, and the new revert commit cancels its effect. The engineer pushes, and teammates simply pull one additional commit — nothing breaks, and the audit trail shows both the mistake and its correction.

Step 5: Later the engineer accidentally runs a hard reset that drops a good commit from the branch. The commit looks lost, but it is only unreferenced, not deleted.

Step 6: The engineer runs git reflog, which lists every prior HEAD position including the one just before the bad reset. They find the good commit's entry and reset back to it, fully restoring the commit. The reflog turned a scary mistake into a two-command recovery.

```
Oct 25, 2026 04:20:02 AM INFO: git reset --soft HEAD~1 -> bad local commit undone, changes staged
Oct 25, 2026 04:30:11 AM WARNING: push999 already pushed+pulled -> must NOT reset
Oct 25, 2026 04:30:40 AM INFO: git revert push999 -> new inverse commit rev000a (history intact)
Oct 25, 2026 04:31:02 AM INFO: push: teammates pull 1 extra commit, nothing breaks
Oct 25, 2026 04:45:03 AM SEVERE: git reset --hard HEAD~1 dropped a GOOD commit
Oct 25, 2026 04:45:30 AM INFO: git reflog -> found HEAD@{1}; reset --hard HEAD@{1} restored it
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  RESET (local, rewrites history):
    good567 ── bad1234 (HEAD)
                  │ git reset --soft/mixed/hard HEAD~1
                  ▼
    good567 (HEAD)        bad1234 changes: staged / unstaged / discarded
    (safe ONLY if bad1234 never pushed)

  REVERT (shared-safe, preserves history):
    base888 ── push999(bug) (HEAD, already pushed)
                  │ git revert push999
                  ▼
    base888 ── push999(bug) ── rev000a(inverse)   <- both kept, audit trail
    push -> teammates pull 1 extra commit, nothing breaks

  REFLOG (recovery after bad reset):
    reset --hard dropped good commit d4e5f6g (unreferenced, not deleted)
      │ git reflog shows HEAD@{1} = d4e5f6g
      ▼ git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
    good commit restored on branch
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Undo Strategy by Commit Visibility (NBI interest) ═══

  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Engineer     │
  │ local repo   │
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ Is the commit already PUSHED/shared?
         │
    ┌────┴─────────────────────┐
    │ NO (local only)           │ YES (shared)
    ▼                           ▼
  ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────┐
  │ git reset       │      │ git revert          │  ← safe for shared history
  │ (soft/mixed/hard│      │ new inverse commit  │
  │  rewrites local)│      │ history preserved   │
  └───────┬────────┘      └─────────┬──────────┘
          │ (if mistake)             │ push
          ▼                          ▼
  ┌────────────────┐         ┌────────────────────┐
  │ git reflog      │         │ Remote (GitHub)     │
  │ recover lost    │         │ teammates pull +1   │
  │ commits (local) │         └────────────────────┘
  └────────────────┘
  Guardrail: branch protection blocks force-push of reset to shared main
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — reset / revert / reflog ═══

  ┌─ Decision + Mode Reference ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  reset --soft  : move ptr; KEEP staged (redo commit)         │
  │  reset --mixed : move ptr; unstage, keep in working dir      │
  │  reset --hard  : move ptr; DISCARD staged + working (danger) │
  │  reset usage   : LOCAL/unshared commits only                 │
  │  revert        : new inverse commit; SHARED-safe; audit trail│
  │  reflog        : local HEAD-movement log; recover lost commits│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── History Pointer Movement ───────────────────────────────

  reset:   good──bad(HEAD)  ──reset HEAD~1──▶  good(HEAD)   [bad dropped]
  revert:  base──bug(HEAD)  ──revert──────▶  base──bug──rev(HEAD) [bug kept]

  ── State Diagram: A Commit After Hard Reset ───────────────

  [on branch] ──reset --hard──→ [unreferenced] ──gc (after expiry)──→ [deleted]
       ▲                              │
       └─── git reflog + reset ───────┘  (recover BEFORE gc)

  ── Command Contracts ──────────────────────────────────────

  git reset --hard <c> Pre: unshared commits  Post: branch+tree at <c>, work lost
  git revert <c>       Pre: any (even shared)  Post: new inverse commit
  git reflog           Pre: local repo         Post: list of HEAD positions

  ── Call Chain (undo + recover) ────────────────────────────

  1. local bad commit  → git reset --soft HEAD~1  (fix + recommit)
  2. pushed bad commit → git revert <hash> → push (shared-safe)
  3. bad hard reset    → git reflog → find HEAD@{n}
  4.                   → git reset --hard HEAD@{n}  (recover)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
git reset and git revert both undo changes, but they work in opposite ways and suit opposite situations. Reset moves the current branch pointer to an earlier commit, which drops the later commits out of the branch — that is a history rewrite. It has three modes: soft keeps the undone changes staged so I can recommit cleanly, mixed keeps them in the working directory unstaged, and hard discards them entirely. Because reset rewrites history, it is safe only on local, unshared commits; if I reset commits that were already pushed and pulled by teammates, I would diverge from their repositories and risk losing their work.

Revert is the non-destructive way to undo. Instead of removing a commit, it computes the inverse of that commit's changes and records them as a brand-new commit on top of the current history. The original commit stays, and the new commit cancels its effect. Because nothing is rewritten and no hashes change, revert is completely safe on shared, already-pushed branches — everyone just pulls one extra commit. For a bank it has the added benefit of preserving the full audit trail, so you can see both the mistake and its correction, which auditors require.

So my rule is straightforward: if the commit is still local and unshared, reset is fine and often cleaner; if the commit is already pushed and others may have it, use revert so I never rewrite shared history. For a mistaken merge that is already public, revert is the correct tool.

git reflog is the safety net that makes Git forgiving. Every time HEAD moves — a commit, checkout, reset, rebase, or merge — Git records the previous position in a local log. So even after a hard reset that appears to destroy commits, those commits are only unreferenced, not immediately deleted, and the reflog still remembers their hashes. I run git reflog, find the entry just before the bad operation, and reset back to it to recover. At National Bank of India this saved me when a hard reset dropped a good interest fix — the reflog turned a scary moment into a two-command recovery. I always note that reflog is local and the unreferenced commits are eventually garbage-collected, so it recovers recent mistakes, not ancient ones, and it is no excuse for hard-resetting or force-pushing shared branches.
